findings.draft_passage: Tom hovered restlessly. "I've got a nice place here," he said, his eyes flashing about. He proposed we go out again; instead we moved toward the porch where four candles flickered on the table in the diminished wind.
findings.source_has: The source has Tom say 'I've got a nice place here' only once, on the porch before entering the house. The second occurrence in the draft is an artifact of compression: the source's interior scene ends with Tom shutting windows, then leading everyone to the dinner porch — no repeated line. The draft duplicated Tom's porch speech and spliced it into the post-interior moment, producing a verbatim repetition that also orphans the phrase 'proposed we go out again' (there is no established 'inside' that they need to leave).
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: Tom appears to repeat word-for-word a remark he made moments ago, and the phrase 'go out again' implies a prior 'going in' that the compressed draft has not clearly staged, making the scene transition unparseable rather than merely less vivid.

findings.draft_passage: They give a better impression than my generalities of those who accepted Gatsby's hospitality and paid him the subtle tribute of knowing nothing whatever about him.
findings.source_has: Source follows this sentence with a multi-paragraph roll-call of named guests (the timetable catalog), to which 'They' refers. The frame sentence exists only as an introduction to that list.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely misled: 'They give a better impression' promises a list that never materialises, leaving the sentence's claim empty and purposeless rather than merely less detailed.

findings.draft_passage: There was nothing to look at except Gatsby's enormous house, so I stared at it, like Kant at his church steeple, for half an hour. Americans, while willing, even eager, to be serfs, have always been obstinate about being peasantry.
findings.source_has: Source anchors the aphorism in a full anecdote: a brewer built the house, tried to get neighbours to thatch their roofs, failed, 'went into an immediate decline,' and his children sold the house — the 'Americans… peasantry' line is the explicit moral of that story.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the aphorism about serfs and peasantry arrives with no narrative setup in the draft, making it impossible to understand what observation it concludes or why it appears at this moment in the text.

findings.draft_passage: There was nothing to look at except Gatsby's enormous house, so I stared at it, like Kant at his church steeple, for half an hour. Americans, while willing, even eager, to be serfs, have always been obstinate about being peasantry.
findings.source_has: Source interposes a full paragraph: a brewer built the house in a 'period craze,' tried to get neighbours to thatch their roofs, was refused, 'took the heart out of his plan to Found a Family,' and died; his children sold the house. The aphorism 'Americans…obstinate about being peasantry' is the explicit moral drawn from that story.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the aphorism arrives with no referent — there is no established situation in the draft involving serfs, peasantry, or feudal refusal — so the sentence reads as a non-sequitur rather than a less-ornamented version of the source.

findings.draft_passage: But the rest offended her—and inarguably because it wasn't a gesture but an emotion.
findings.source_has: Source immediately precedes this with Daisy saying 'I like her, I think she's lovely' about the movie star under the white-plum tree, establishing the thing she *did* like before the contrastive 'but the rest offended her.'
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'but the rest' requires an established contrast (something she liked), which has been cut entirely from the draft; without it, the sentence's logical pivot has no other side and 'the rest' has no defined referent.

findings.draft_passage: the conductor to familiar faces: "Hot! … Hot! … Hot! … Is it hot enough for you?"
findings.source_has: "Hot!" said the conductor to familiar faces. "Some weather! … Hot! … Hot! … Hot! … Is it hot enough for you?"
findings.gate_test_answer: A competent reader is genuinely confused: the sentence 'the conductor to familiar faces: ...' has no main verb and cannot be parsed as a grammatical sentence — it is not merely a less-ornamented version of the original.

findings.draft_passage: But the rest offended her—and inarguably because it wasn't a gesture but an emotion.
findings.source_has: "I like her," said Daisy, "I think she's lovely." But the rest offended her—and inarguably because it wasn't a gesture but an emotion.
findings.gate_test_answer: A competent reader is genuinely confused: the adversative 'but' requires a preceding positive claim for contrast, but the draft cuts Daisy's approval of the movie star entirely, leaving 'but the rest offended her' floating with no antecedent positive proposition to push against.

findings.draft_passage: "They were out in the open at last and Gatsby was content."
findings.source_has: They were out in the open at last and Gatsby was content. [unquoted narratorial statement, not dialogue]
findings.gate_test_answer: A competent reader is genuinely confused: the compression has accidentally enclosed the narrator's aside in quotation marks, making it appear to be spoken dialogue with no identifiable speaker, immediately after Tom's question and before Daisy's response.

findings.draft_passage: "They were out in the open at last and Gatsby was content." Daisy begged for self-control.
findings.source_has: They were out in the open at last and Gatsby was content. [narrator's statement, unquoted] Daisy begged for self-control.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader seeing quotation marks around 'They were out in the open at last and Gatsby was content' will be genuinely confused about who is speaking this line and what its meaning is, since it reads as a character's utterance when it is actually Nick's authorial commentary with no speaker.

findings.draft_passage: she swore that her sister had never seen Gatsby, that she was completely happy with her husband, that she had been into no mischief whatever.
findings.source_has: swore that her sister had never seen Gatsby, that her sister was completely happy with her husband, that her sister had been into no mischief whatever
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the second and third 'she' could refer to Catherine (the paragraph's grammatical subject) rather than to the sister, making it ambiguous whose marital happiness and misconduct is being sworn to.

findings.draft_passage: 'Go on! Why, my God! they used to go there by the hundreds.' He took off his glasses and wiped them, outside and in. 'The poor son-of-a-bitch,' he said.
findings.source_has: It was the man with owl-eyed glasses whom I had found marvelling over Gatsby's books in the library … Owl-eyes spoke to me by the gate. 'I couldn't get to the house,' he remarked … 'Go on!' He started. 'Why, my God! they used to go there by the hundreds.' … 'The poor son-of-a-bitch,' he said.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the voice delivering these lines has no established identity in the draft — the character's arrival and identification were cut — so the exclamation and epitaph float without any speaker the reader can place.
